title: Synagogue
description: Place of worship for Jews or Samaritans
wiki_lead:
A synagogue or synagog, 'Beit Kneset'—"house of gathering" in Hebrew, also called a shul (meaning school in Yiddish) or a temple, is a place of worship for Jews or Samaritans.
It serves as a house of prayer. It includes a main sanctuary with the Torah ark where the Torah scrolls are kept (called a Holy Closet aron qodesh (Hebrew: אָרוֹן קׄדֶש) by Ashkenazi Jews and a hekhal (היכל) by Sephardic Jews), and a stage called bema in front of it as well as raised galleries for female worshipers. Synagogues have religious services or ceremonies such as Daily prayers, Shabbat prayers (Saturday) weddings, bar and bat mitzvahs. Synagogues often also contain study rooms, social halls, administrative and charitable offices, classrooms for religious and Hebrew studies, and spaces for community gatherings. They frequently display commemorative, historic, or modern artwork alongside items of Jewish historical significance or exhibits about the synagogue itself.
Synagogues are buildings used for Jewish prayer, study, assembly, and reading of the Torah. The Torah (Pentateuch or Five Books of Moses) is traditionally read in its entirety over a period of a year in weekly portions during services, or in some synagogues on a triennial cycle. However, the edifice of a synagogue as such is not essential for holding Jewish worship. Halakha (Jewish law from the Mishnah—the "Oral Torah") states that communal Jewish worship can be carried out wherever a minyan, a group of at least 10 Jewish adults, is assembled, often (but not necessarily) led by a rabbi. This minyan is the essence of Jewish communal worship, which can also be conducted alone or with fewer than ten people, but that excludes certain prayers as well as communal Torah reading. In terms of its specific ritual and liturgical functions, the synagogue does not replace the long-destroyed Temple in Jerusalem.
Any Jew or group of Jews can build a synagogue. Synagogues have been constructed by ancient Jewish leaders, wealthy patrons, and as part of a wide range of human institutions, including secular educational institutions, governments, and hotels. They have been built by the entire Jewish community living in a particular village or region, or by sub-groups of Jewish people organized by occupation, tradition/background (e.g., the Sephardic, Yemenite, Romaniote or Persian Jews of a town), style of religious observance (e.g., Orthodox or Reform synagogues), or by the followers of a particular rabbi, such as the shtiebelekh (Yiddish: שטיבעלעך, romanized: shtibelekh, singular שטיבל shtibl) of Hasidic Judaism.

It serves as a house of prayer. It includes a main sanctuary with the Torah ark where the Torah scrolls are kept (called a Holy Closet aron qodesh (Hebrew: אָרוֹן קׄדֶש) by Ashkenazi Jews and a hekhal (היכל) by Sephardic Jews), and a stage called bema in front of it as well as raised galleries for female worshipers. Synagogues have religious services or ceremonies such as Daily prayers, Shabbat prayers (Saturday) weddings, bar and bat mitzvahs. Synagogues often also contain study rooms, social halls, administrative and charitable offices, classrooms for religious and Hebrew studies, and spaces for community gatherings. They frequently display commemorative, historic, or modern artwork alongside items of Jewish historical significance or exhibits about the synagogue itself.
Synagogues are buildings used for Jewish prayer, study, assembly, and reading of the Torah. The Torah (Pentateuch or Five Books of Moses) is traditionally read in its entirety over a period of a year in weekly portions during services, or in some synagogues on a triennial cycle. However, the edifice of a synagogue as such is not essential for holding Jewish worship. Halakha (Jewish law from the Mishnah—the "Oral Torah") states that communal Jewish worship can be carried out wherever a minyan, a group of at least 10 Jewish adults, is assembled, often (but not necessarily) led by a rabbi. This minyan is the essence of Jewish communal worship, which can also be conducted alone or with fewer than ten people, but that excludes certain prayers as well as communal Torah reading. In terms of its specific ritual and liturgical functions, the synagogue does not replace the long-destroyed Temple in Jerusalem.
Any Jew or group of Jews can build a synagogue. Synagogues have been constructed by ancient Jewish leaders, wealthy patrons, and as part of a wide range of human institutions, including secular educational institutions, governments, and hotels. They have been built by the entire Jewish community living in a particular village or region, or by sub-groups of Jewish people organized by occupation, tradition/background (e.g., the Sephardic, Yemenite, Romaniote or Persian Jews of a town), style of religious observance (e.g., Orthodox or Reform synagogues), or by the followers of a particular rabbi, such as the shtiebelekh (Yiddish: שטיבעלעך, romanized: shtibelekh, singular שטיבל shtibl) of Hasidic Judaism.


Terminology
The Hebrew term is bet knesset (בית כנסת) or "house of assembly". The Koine Greek-derived word synagogue (συναγωγή) also means "assembly" and is commonly used in English, with its earliest mention in the 1st century Theodotos inscription in Jerusalem. Ashkenazi Jews have traditionally used the Yiddish term shul (from the Greek schola, which is also the source of the English "school") in everyday speech, and many continue to do so in English.
Sephardi Jews and Romaniote Jews generally use the term kal (from the Hebrew qahal "community"). Spanish and Portuguese Jews call the synagogue an esnoga and Portuguese Jews may call it a sinagoga. Persian Jews and some Karaite Jews also use the term kenesa, which is derived from Aramaic, and some Mizrahi Jews use kenis or qnis, the Arabic word for a synagogue, or ṣla, the Arabic word for prayer.


History


Origins
The origins of the synagogue are obscure. Scholarly opinion has been divided among several views. The first holds that the synagogue arose after Josiah's reform of 622/1 BCE banned sacrifice outside the First Temple in Jerusalem. The second, long the most widely held, holds that it was created during the Babylonian exile as an alternative form of worship after the Temple's destruction in 587/6 BCE. The third view traces it to Ezra's public reading of the Torah in 5th-century BCE Jerusalem as narrated in the biblical Book of Nehemiah. Other scholars have proposed an origin among diaspora communities in Hellenistic Egypt.
Historian and archaeologist Lee I. Levine argues that the synagogue developed gradually between the 5th and 1st centuries BCE. In biblical times, communal life centered on the city gate and the open space beside it, which served as a marketplace, a courtroom, a venue for delivering prophecies, a forum for public assemblies, and sometimes a site of worship. Archaeological evidence, mainly from pagan coastal cities, shows that in the Hellenistic period gates became simple passageways between towers. In Levin's view, the activities once held there moved into what became known as the synagogue. Levine suggests the institution emerged more or less simultaneously in Judea, where the old gate setting was disappearing, and in the diaspora, where Jews could not use the gates of pagan cities for communal life.


Second Temple period
The earliest firm evidence for the synagogue comes from the Second Temple period, and more specifically, from 3rd-century BCE Ptolemaic Egypt, where several inscriptions and papyri in Koine Greek mention a προσευχή, proseukhē, 'house of prayer' (plural: προσευχαί, proseukhái). The oldest dedications date to the reign of Ptolemy III Euergetes, king of Egypt between 246 and 221 BCE. Egyptian Jews commonly dedicated their prayer houses on behalf of the reigning king and queen. No synagogue building has yet been found in Egypt. The oldest known synagogue building is the Delos Synagogue on the Aegean island of Delos, which was in use at least from the first century BCE. It is the only pre-70 diaspora structure widely identified as a synagogue.
Synagogues are attested in the Land of Israel after they appeared in the diaspora, with the earliest known example dating from the late 2nd century BCE. Earlier Jewish and pagan writings are almost silent about synagogues in this region. Ben Sira and the books of Maccabees do not mention it, and where synagōgē appears in 1 Maccabees, it refers to a group of people, not a building. For a long time, few sites supported the existence of synagogue buildings in the regions of Judea and Galilee before the destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE. In the Herodian palace-fort hilltop complexes of Masada and Herodium, the synagogues were not built as such but were adapted by rebels during the First Jewish Revolt and the Bar Kokhba Revolt. The first site to become generally accepted as a purpose-built synagogue was the Gamla Synagogue in Gamla, an ancient Jewish town in the Golan Heights, with proposed dates ranging from the mid-first century BCE to roughly the turn of the era.
Excavation has since widened the picture. Proposed Second Temple-era synagogues now include Khirbet Badd 'Isa (in Modi'in Illit), Umm el-'Umdan (in Modi'in), where a Hasmonean-period building was succeeded by a Herodian one, and the Migdal Synagogue (in ancient Magdala) with its two phases. Their typical layout is an open hall lined with benches, with a roof carried on interior colonnades. Other proposals remain disputed, including the public structure at Horvat 'Ethri and small rural sites such as Horvat Diab and Tel Rekhesh. The Theodotus inscription, dated to between the first century BCE and the first century CE, points to a synagogue serving a Greek-speaking community in Jerusalem.
By the first century CE, the synagogue was the central communal institution of Jewish communities in both Judaea and the diaspora. Large cities such as Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Rome had several, and smaller Jewish communities throughout the Roman Empire probably had at least one each, so it is probable that hundreds, perhaps thousands, existed. Philo and Josephus mention lavishly adorned synagogues in Alexandria and in Antioch, respectively.
Diaspora synagogues varied in name and practice. They went by many names in Greek, including proseukhē, synagōgē, hieron, sabbateion, and didaskaleion. This diversity arose partly because the founding communities had no model to follow, and partly because each community adopted patterns from its surrounding culture, in organization as well as in architecture. Most used Greek in inscriptions and official titles, and honored benefactors in Greco-Roman fashion. Yet the institution remained distinctively Jewish, centered on the reading of scripture.
In both Judaea and the diaspora, the main religious activity was public Torah reading. In the diaspora, at least, this took place above all on Shabbat, Judaism's weekly day of rest. In the diaspora, synagogues also safeguarded sacred books and money collected for the Jerusalem Temple, and many had halls for communal meals. The Book of Acts describes a Shabbat service at Antioch of Pisidia in which readings from the Torah and Nevi'im were followed by an invitation to address the congregation. A synagogue could also serve as a court, school, hostel, or venue for political meetings. Roman decrees preserved by Josephus upheld the Jews' right to assemble, collect funds, and dine together, even in Rome, where other religious associations were banned.

Levine rejects the once-common view of the synagogue as a rival to the Jerusalem Temple or as a creation of the Pharisaic movement. In Judea, it held no special sanctity during the Second Temple period. Several sources show priests prominent in its affairs, and no evidence connects the early synagogue with the Pharisees.


Talmudic period

Following the destruction of the Temple, the synagogue became the focal point of Jewish worship and communal life. Lester L. Grabbe writes: "The rise of the synagogue was a fortuitous but vital development which paved the way for a post-temple Judaism which became necessary after 70 [...] Synagogues were not planned as a substitute for the temple but they were a useful vehicle to make the transition." Over time, prayers, rituals, and customs once performed in the Temple were adapted for synagogue use. Traditional forms of synagogal worship, including sermons and the reading of scripture, were preserved, while new forms of worship, such as piyyut and organized prayer, developed. Rabbinic instruction, however, maintained that certain practices should remain exclusive to the Temple. The Mishnah directed prayers toward Jerusalem, and most synagogues face the Temple site rather than mirroring its orientation, establishing them as extensions of its sanctity, not replicas.
During Late antiquity (third to seventh century CE), literary sources attest to the existence of a large number of synagogues across the Roman-Byzantine and Sasanian Empires. Archaeological evidence indicates the presence of synagogues in at least thirteen places across the diaspora, spanning from Dura-Europos in Syria to Elche in Hispania (modern-day Spain). An especially sizable and monumental synagogue dating from this period is the Sardis Synagogue. Additionally, many inscriptions pertaining to synagogues and their officials have been discovered.
In the Land of Israel, late antiquity witnessed a significant increase in synagogue construction, in Galilee and Golan in the north and the southern hills of Judea, in the south. Each synagogue was constructed according to the means and religious customs of the local community. Notable examples include Capernaum, Bar'am, Beth Alpha, Maoz Haim, Meroth and Nabratein in the north, and Eshtemoa, Susya, Anim, and Maon in the south.
There is epigraphic and archaeological evidence that a synagogue dating to the third century existed to serve a significant Jewish community in Volubilis, capital of the former Kingdom of Mauretania, in what is now Morocco.


Middle Ages
Rabbi and philosopher Maimonides (1138–1204) described the various customs in his day with respect to local synagogues:

Originating during the Second Temple period, synagogues functioned as assemblies for public reading of scripture and communal gatherings, distinct from the Temple's sacrificial cult. Archaeological evidence confirms the existence of synagogues from the first century BCE, with structures identified at sites like Gamla, Masada, and Magdala in ancient Judea, featuring simple basalt benches and orientations toward Jerusalem. Following the Roman destruction of the Second Temple in 70 CE, synagogues assumed greater prominence as the primary venue for Jewish worship, emphasizing prayer, scriptural exposition, and ethical instruction over ritual sacrifice. This shift enabled Judaism's adaptation and survival in the diaspora, where synagogues became hubs for maintaining religious identity amid dispersion and persecution. Architecturally diverseâfrom austere ancient halls to ornate medieval and modern edifices incorporating elements like Torah arks, bimahs for readings, and ritual objects such as eternal lightsâsynagogues reflect regional influences while adhering to core functions of assembly and sanctity. Today, synagogues worldwide sustain Jewish continuity through daily and Sabbath services, lifecycle events, charitable activities, and cultural preservation, accommodating Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, and other denominations with varying liturgical emphases. Despite historical desecrations and destructions, including during the Holocaust, their resilience underscores Judaism's decentralized, text-centered ethos, privileging communal devotion over centralized priesthood or temple dependency.
